items.title: Methodology for selecting an information source for online diagnostics of cutting tool edge condition
items.abstract: The work focuses on the development of a method for selecting diagnostic features in the milling of materials with significantly different properties. The use of two very different materials allowed for better generalization of the conclusions. The research concentrated on steel and composite materials, defined as combinations of two or more materials with diverse chemical and mechanical properties. A method for assessing the usefulness of measured physical quantities for predicting tool wear using machine learning techniques was proposed. Both vibration signals and cutting forces were considered, but the proposed method is general. The study implements artificial intelligence methods through the practical deployment of multiple machine‑learning models trained on vibration‑ and force‑based features. The methodology is based on a measure of the significance of data partitioning into subsets created from forces and vibration accelerations, combined with a large set of supervised machine learning methods, including classification and regression algorithms with various hyperparameters. This approach enables a relatively objective statistical assessment of the usefulness of a given physical quantity in monitoring tool condition.

items.title: Mixture-of-Quants: Hosting High-Precision LLMs at Low-Precision Memory Bandwidth
items.abstract: Serving a Large Language Model (LLM) to a single user is bound by memory bandwidth: every generated token requires the entire weight set to be read from memory. Quantising weights to 4 bits halves the traffic of an 8-bit model but measurably degrades reasoning. We propose Mixture-of-Quants (MoQ), which exploits the observation that at each decode step the difference between the 4-bit model's two highest token probabilities indicates whether the 8-bit weights would produce a different output. By default, MoQ decodes each new token at 4 bits. Only when the top-2 softmax margin falls below a threshold is the token recomputed from the 8-bit weights. The 8-bit weights are stored as the 4-bit plane plus a 4-bit residual, so the store is the same size as an 8-bit model but only 4 bits per weight are read on the majority of tokens. Across three 27B–31B parameter architectures and \(\approx\) 300,000 scored positions, the margin predicts 4-bit/8-bit disagreement with AUROC of 0.93–0.95, catching 80% of disagreements whilst escalating 12%–16% of positions. On 3,000 paired SuperGPQA questions with a 32,768-token reasoning budget, escalating 31% of tokens lifts accuracy from 57.2% (4-bit) to 58.9%, matching the 8-bit model (58.9%, exact McNemar \(p = 1.000\)) and beating 4-bit at the same significance as the 4-bit/8-bit gap itself (\(p = 0.010\)). By physically relocating weights between HBM3 (3,850 GB/s) and Grace LPDDR (84 GB/s) on GH200 superchips, we show MoQ's throughput advantage over 8-bit rises monotonically from 1.38\(\times\) to 1.70\(\times\) as bandwidth falls, and that placing the rarely-read residual plane in slow memory is 3.9\(\times\) faster than spreading the same bytes uniformly, a trade a flat 8-bit model cannot make.

items.title: MORAL RIGHTS OF AUTHORS IN THE AGE OF AI-GENERATED CONTENT
items.abstract: The technology of Generative AI is now capable not only of writing, painting, and composing, but even transforming the work of others. While India's Copyright Act, 1957 was framed taking humans into consideration as the creators, yet there is an exception for Computer Generated Works and an additional set of Moral Rights provided for in Section 57. The present article enquires into the possibility of using these provisions to safeguard the human creators in case AI transforms or creates a work. It contemplates that while the Copyright Act provides for a sufficient framework for the purpose, it lacks provisions regarding the role of humans in the creation, alteration by AI, misattribution, and proving the same. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Authorship, Moral Rights, Section 57, Copyright Act, 1957, Generative AI, Right of Integrity, Right of Attribution.

items.title: More Alerts, Less Prevention? A Computational Study of Hazard Detection, Response Capacity and Threshold Choice in Occupational Health and Safety
items.abstract: AI-enabled hazard detection is usually judged by whether it finds risky conditions. Prevention requires another step: somebody must have the time, authority and competence to respond. This article evaluates how that second step alters the interpretation of predictive safety performance. It reports a factorial computational experiment derived from a doctoral study of AI in occupational health and safety (OHS). Across 54 simulated operating conditions, five alert thresholds and 200 replications per condition, a score-based detector classifies 5,000 opportunities per replication. The design varies hazardous-opportunity prevalence (1%, 5% and 15%), score separation (1, 2 and 3), drift (0 and 0.75) and nominal response probability (0.40, 0.65 and 0.90), with response capacity limited to 500 alerts. At the reference threshold of 1.5, one 5%-prevalence, separation-2, no-drift condition yields mean residual hazardous opportunities of 180.8, 138.2 and 95.7 across the three response assumptions. With the same detector and nominal 65% response, imposing drift raises mean residual opportunities from 138.2 to 185.5. A sensitivity calculation also changes the preferred threshold when the relative weight of unresolved hazards and false alerts changes. The simulation shows why sensitivity, precision, workload and verified action belong in the same OHS decision model. All numerical data are computer-generated. The study does not report a deployed machine-learning system, workplace incidents, observed worker behaviour or injury reduction. Its contribution is a transparent stress test of the management choices that connect detection to prevention.

items.title: MOS: Towards Effective Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection through Mixture-of-Experts Tuning of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Smart contract vulnerabilities pose significant security risks to blockchain systems, potentially leading to severe financial losses. Existing methods face several limitations: (1) Program analysis-based approaches heavily rely on predefined patterns, lacking flexibility and adaptability to new vulnerability types; (2) Deep learning-based methods lack explanations for their detection results; (3) Large language model-based approaches suffer from high false positive rates. To address these challenges, we propose MOS, a smart contract vulnerability detection framework based on mixture-of-experts tuning (MOE-Tuning) of large language models. First, we conduct Continual Pre-training on a large-scale smart contract dataset to provide a domain-enhanced initialization for the subsequent MOE-Tuning process. Second, to provide reliable explanations for detected vulnerabilities, we construct a high-quality MOE-Tuning dataset through a multi-stage pipeline combining large language model generation and expert verification. Third, we design a vulnerability-aware routing mechanism that activates the most relevant expert networks by analyzing code features and their matching degree with experts, addressing the limitation of predefined patterns in program analysis approaches. Finally, we extend the feed-forward layers of the LLM after Continual Pre-training into multiple parallel expert networks, each specializing in specific vulnerability patterns. We also employ a dual-objective loss function: one for optimizing vulnerability detection and explanation performance, and another for balancing expert utilization through an auxiliary loss based on the scaled dot product of expert assignment frequencies and average routing probabilities, thereby improving model performance in complex vulnerability scenarios. Extensive experiments show that MOS consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in four foundational and historically significant vulnerability types (Reentrancy, Timestamp, Integer Overflow/Underflow, Delegatecall) with average improvements of 6.38% in F1 score and 4.84% in accuracy. The vulnerability explanations generated by MOS also demonstrate high quality, achieving positive ratings (scores of 3 and 4 on a 4-point scale) of 82.96%, 85.21% and 94.58% for correctness, completeness, and conciseness, respectively, through a combined approach of human evaluation and LLM evaluation. Extensibility experiments show that MOS effectively handles new vulnerability types (Access Control, Price Oracle Manipulation, Logic Errors, Lack of Input Validation, Slippage, and Risky First Deposit), consistently outperforming all baseline methods across six additional vulnerability categories. MOS achieved an average F1 score of 83.94% and an average accuracy of 87.82%, demonstrating its strong extensibility and flexibility in handling new vulnerabilities.

items.title: MSI-3, an improved version of the MSI application that includes both fungal and bacterial identifications for MALDI-ToF spectra
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-ToF MS) is now central to routine diagnostics, enabling accurate identification of microbial species. We assessed the performance of MSI-3, the updated release of the free online mass spectrometry identification (MSI) platform that now supports bacterial, in addition to fungal, identification. MSI-3 was benchmarked against MSI-2 and the Bruker MALDI Biotyper using two fungal data sets: (i) a reference panel of 669 sequenced isolates (Panel 1), and (ii) a real-world set of user-submitted spectra (Panel 2). MSI-3 and MSI-2 demonstrated equivalent performance across all fungal groups in Panel 1, with 97.8% (mean of 892/912) concordance at the species or species complex level, and a massive added value compared to the Bruker database for filamentous fungi (from about 41% to about 98%). MSI-3 exhibited slightly longer identification times than MSI-2 (1.52 vs 0.84 s per spectrum), but remained compatible with real-time online usage. The increased identification time is offset by a twofold expansion of the reference database and algorithmic improvements. In Panel 2, MSI-3 achieved comparable performance to Bruker for bacterial and yeast spectra, and outperformed Bruker for filamentous fungi, especially Aspergillus spp., Fusarium spp., and dermatophytes. A new “uninterpretable” category was introduced in MSI-3 to flag potential mixed or poor-quality spectra, facilitating result interpretation. Overall, MSI-3 marks a substantial advance in the MSI platform, uniting flexibility, broad taxonomic coverage, and artificial intelligence (AI) readiness. Its combined use with Bruker enhances diagnostic performance, positioning MSI-3 as a powerful and scalable standard for microbial identification in clinical and research settings. IMPORTANCE This article highlights the major importance of MSI-3 as a significant advancement in microbial identification using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-ToF MS). The expansion of the platform to bacterial identification, together with its already established fungal database and improved algorithms, now enables users to analyze mixed projects through a single workflow without additional sample handling or database switching. Used by more than 500 users worldwide, MSI-3 provides improved diagnostic performance, particularly for filamentous fungi, while offering a flexible and scalable solution for both clinical and research microbiology.

items.title: Multi-Horizon Future Discovery for Physics-Informed Exploration
items.abstract: Exploration in physical control environments requires agents to identify actions whose consequences reveal previously unexplored aspects of the underlying dynamics. However, many intrinsic motivation methods rely on immediate prediction errors, state novelty, or local physical changes, which may overlook informative outcomes that emerge across extended temporal horizons. We investigate whether learning structured representations of reachable futures can provide a more effective basis for exploration. To this end, we introduce Hamiltonian Temporal Contrastive Curiosity (HTC$^2$), a framework that combines multi-horizon temporal representation learning with Hamiltonian phase-space structure. A horizon-conditioned contrastive critic learns temporal relationships from future-state pairs sampled within the same episode. The distance between positive-pair representations is then used as an intrinsic reward, encouraging the agent to explore futures that remain insufficiently organized in the learned representation. To incorporate information about physical dynamics, we additionally modulate this reward using bounded multi-step Hamiltonian variation, rather than directly rewarding changes in the Hamiltonian itself. We integrate HTC$^2$ with both Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and evaluate it across six DeepMind Control Suite tasks. Comparisons with ICM, RIDE, E3B, Plan2Explore, and a single-step Hamiltonian curiosity baseline are complemented by state-coverage evaluations, component ablations, and phase-space diagnostics to characterize the contributions of temporal learning and physical structure to exploratory behavior.

items.title: Multiproperty optimization of therapeutic antibodies through sequence editing via large language model and reinforcement learning
items.abstract: Discovering antibodies with multiple beneficial properties is essential for therapeutic drug development, but experimentally identified antibodies require further optimization. Joint optimization remains challenging because sequence space is vast, annotations are sparse and property tradeoffs are common. Herein, we propose AbOptimizer, a reinforcement learning framework for multiproperty antibody optimization through parallel multisite sequence editing. AbOptimizer identifies promising editing sites and edit actions, including ‘reservation’, ‘substitution’ and optional ‘insertion’ or ‘deletion’, before recommending mutations from protein language models, while surrogate evaluation and Pareto rewards shape policy training. We evaluate AbOptimizer on three therapeutic antibodies across multiproperty, data-limited and indel-inclusive optimization. In silico, AbOptimizer improves optimized properties and outperforms baseline methods. In vitro, selected variants show affinity-specificity co-optimization for emibetuzumab, improved affinity and specificity with largely maintained thermal stability for siltuximab, and indel-inclusive affinity optimization for trastuzumab. These results validate AbOptimizer as a practical framework for therapeutic antibody optimization. This study presents AbOptimizer, a computational framework that edits antibody sequences to improve multiple therapeutic properties. Tests on three antibodies show improved affinity, specificity and stability-related profiles.

items.title: MUSE: Revealing Responsiveness Gaps of LLM Tutors on Multiple-Solution Programming Problems
items.abstract: When a problem admits multiple valid solutions, effective tutoring requires building on a student's strategy while introducing alternatives at appropriate points. However, whether LLM tutors can support this flexibility by appropriately responding to students' diverse solution approaches remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce MUSE: Multi-solution Understanding and Simulation Environment, a controlled environment for simulating student-tutor conversations on multiple-solution programming problems. Grounded in learning science on responsive instruction and multiple-solution learning, we investigate which solutions LLM tutors prefer, how they respond to students' approaches, and how they transition between solutions. Experiments suggest that LLM tutors exhibit systematic preferences among valid solutions, often favoring brute-force approaches when not providing general advice. More concerningly, tutors often impose these preferences, redirecting students toward their own preferred approach rather than supporting the student's. Yet this tendency reverses once a solution is completed: tutors often remain anchored to the existing approach when a stronger alternative could deepen understanding, and sometimes even transition to a less optimal approach. Thus, tutors struggle both to build on students' reasoning when appropriate and to extend their reasoning when beneficial. Promisingly, targeted post-training improves both tutor responsiveness and transitions toward more optimal solutions.

items.title: Navigating catastrophic airway hemorrhage and cardiac arrest during bronchoscopy in an octogenarian with AECOPD: a critical care nursing case study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Bronchoscopic biopsy in elderly patients with Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (AECOPD) presents high procedural risks. This case study analyzes the critical care nursing trajectory of an 76-year-old patient who survived a massive endobronchial hemorrhage and subsequent in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) during an interventional procedure. Resentation An 76-year-old male with severe COPD (FEV1 40% predicted) and hypertension underwent diagnostic bronchoscopy. Immediately following mucosal biopsy, the patient developed massive hemorrhage (approx. 300 mL), leading to acute asphyxia and pulseless electrical activity (PEA). The critical care nursing team initiated a rapid response, facilitating emergency tracheal intubation and localized hemostasis using epinephrine irrigation. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved after 6 min of advanced life support. Nursing interventions The nursing management focused on three critical phases: (1) Crisis Resource Management (CRM): utilizing rapid situational awareness to clear the airway and coordinate multidisciplinary resuscitation; (2) Post-ROSC Stabilization: implementing lung-protective ventilation and precise cuff pressure titration (25–30 cmH 2 O) to prevent re-bleeding and ventilator-associated complications; and (3) Secondary Prevention: managing the delicate balance between necessary anticoagulation for cardiovascular comorbidities and the risk of recurrent pulmonary hemorrhage during the recovery phase. Conclusion This case report documents the successful resuscitation of an 76-year-old male with severe AECOPD (FEV1 40% predicted) who developed massive endobronchial hemorrhage (~ 300 mL) and in-hospital cardiac arrest (pulseless electrical activity) during diagnostic bronchoscopy. Detailed preoperative risk stratification, intraoperative crisis resource management, and post-ROSC intensive care nursing interventions are described and analyzed. A comprehensive geriatric assessment, complete resuscitation parameters, functional outcomes, and a comparative discussion with existing literature on bronchoscopy-related airway hemorrhage are provided. A nine-phase nursing decision-making framework for high-risk bronchoscopy in elderly AECOPD patients is proposed. This report highlights the critical role of nursing-led situational awareness, structured crisis management, and dynamic hemodynamic titration in navigating catastrophic cardiopulmonary events in high-risk elderly populations. Clinical trial number not applicable.

items.title: Navigating the Ethical and Regulatory Landscape of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems represents one of the most profound shifts in modern medicine, promising enhanced diagnostics, personalized treatments, and operational efficiencies. However, this transformation is not without its complexities, particularly in the realms of ethics and regulatory compliance. This narrative review synthesizes current literature, policy frameworks, and global case studies to examine the ethical challenges—such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, transparency, and equity—and the regulatory mechanisms designed to address them. Drawing from diverse sources including WHO guidelines, EU AI Act, FDA policies, and India’s National Strategy for AI, the article highlights the tension between innovation and safeguards. Key findings underscore the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to foster trustworthy AI, emphasizing human-centered design, inclusive data practices, and adaptive regulations. With the global AI healthcare market projected to exceed $500 billion by 2032, this review advocates for a balanced approach that prioritizes patient autonomy, societal equity, and sustainable development. Ultimately, ethical and regulatory frameworks must evolve in tandem with technology to ensure AI serves as a tool for healing rather than division.

items.title: Neodymium Oxide-Induced Male Reproductive Dysfunction in Mice Is Associated with TFR1/FTH1 Axis Dysregulation and Ferroptosis-Related Alterations: A Proteomics-Based Study
items.abstract: Growing concerns regarding the environmental and occupational health risks associated with rare earth elements have highlighted the importance of elucidating the mechanisms underlying neodymium oxide (Nd2O3)-induced male reproductive toxicity. In this study, male C57BL/6J mice were exposed to Nd2O3 at concentrations of 250, 500, or 1000 mg/m3 through nose-only inhalation for 2 h/day over 90 consecutive days. The effects of Nd2O3 exposure on male reproductive function were investigated using histopathological examination, sperm analysis, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), quantitative proteomics, bioinformatics analysis, Western blotting, and biochemical assays. Nd2O3 exposure was associated with testicular histopathological alterations, decreased sperm count, and increased sperm abnormalities. Quantitative proteomic analysis identified 892 differentially expressed proteins enriched in biological processes and pathways associated with spermatogenesis, ribosome function, endoplasmic reticulum protein processing, programmed cell death, iron uptake and transport, lipid metabolism, and ferroptosis. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis further identified a ferroptosis-associated module containing ACSL4, HMOX1, TF, HMGB1, and SIRT1. TEM qualitatively revealed apparent mitochondrial shrinkage and cristae alterations in testicular cells, compatible with ferroptosis-associated ultrastructural changes. Western blotting demonstrated dose-dependent upregulation of TFR1 and downregulation of FTH1 following Nd2O3 exposure. Moreover, Nd2O3 exposure decreased serum testosterone and estradiol levels, increased total iron, Fe2+, malondialdehyde, and 4-hydroxynonenal levels, and depleted reduced glutathione in both serum and testicular tissues, indicating disrupted iron homeostasis, impaired antioxidant capacity, and enhanced lipid peroxidation. Collectively, these proteomic, molecular, biochemical, and morphological findings indicate that Nd2O3-induced male reproductive dysfunction is associated with TFR1/FTH1 axis dysregulation, disrupted iron homeostasis, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis-related alterations.

items.title: Neuromorphic Computing in Human-System Interaction: A Scoping Review of Recent Developments, Key Challenges, and Future Research Opportunities
items.abstract: This review examines recent advances in neuromorphic computing for human-system interaction (HSI). Inspired by the nervous system, neuromorphic computing utilizes spiking neural network models, event-driven processing, and biomimetic hardware to enable ultra-low power computing. The review analyzes 35 scientific papers published up to May 2026, classifying applications into five categories: brain-computer interface and healthcare applications, human-robot collaboration, neuromorphic synapse and hardware, affective computing and emotion recognition, and neuromorphic sensors and human-machine interfaces. Compared to conventional computing techniques, neuromorphic computing exhibits low-power consumption and faster processing. Recent advancements in neuromorphic computers include the development of memristors, flexible synaptic devices, and self-powered sensory systems. However, challenges such as standardization of datasets, system scalability, hardware-software integration, system explainability, data security, and data privacy can be recognized as the future research topics of neuromorphic computing for HSI. Overall, neuromorphic computing provides a potential HSI solution for a safer, more intelligent, and more human-centered future.

items.title: Next Lab to Next Leaders: Student-led Innovation and Leadership
items.abstract: Next Lab demonstrates that a student-led, studio-based innovation ecosystem can function as a leadership laboratory, where agency and ethical judgment develop through paid, real-stakes design work with external partners in emerging technologies. Grounded in heutagogy and agentic leadership, Next Lab at Arizona State University engages students in interdisciplinary, socially impactful design challenges that integrate artificial intelligence (AI), spatial computing, and game technologies. This chapter examines the lab’s studio-based model through institutional context, collaborative case studies, and evidence from alumni outcomes. Drawing on both qualitative reflections and survey data, the chapter shows how real-world, paid design work cultivates adaptive leadership, technical fluency, and ethical foresight. Together, these findings position the Next Lab model as a transferable framework for preparing graduates to navigate complex technological and societal futures.

items.title: NOT EVEN THE GODS KNOW: TEN POSSIBLE DESTINIES OF HUMANITY IN THE FACE OF EXTRATERRESTRIAL PRESENCE
items.abstract: Given the premise, supported by recent institutional, scientific and journalistic milestones, that Extraterrestrial Intelligences (ETIs) maintain a current and verifiable presence on Earth, this theoretical-hypothesis paper develops and defends the thesis that the question “what should be done?” admits no single, definitive or conclusive answer. Grounded in established epistemological traditions — situated knowledges, paradigmatic incommensurability and the underdetermination of theory by evidence — the paper argues that each observer’s answer depends on constitutive, experiential and contextual variables that differentially shape diagnosis, prognosis and attitude. The author’s biographical and investigative trajectory — four decades of ufological research documented in earlier peer-reviewed work and in two public pre-tragedy manifestos (2019 and 2022), including the paradigmatic case of Donato Cervantes and the Homeric Theater Hypothesis — centrally marked by the murder of his son by military police officers in November 2024, is explicitly positioned as a legitimate interpretive lens, not as an impossible neutrality. On this basis, ten scenarios for humanity’s destiny are analyzed with deliberately equivalent argumentative weight — inaction; open, massive contact; nuclear war; other human causes (resource depletion, global warming, genetically engineered virus); natural catastrophe; technical preparation for survival; replacement by artificial intelligence; inner transformation toward a “new human”; physical rescue by ETIs; and direct destruction by ETIs — each supported by multidisciplinary evidence (existential-risk literature, the twelve-criteria methodology for assessing contactee authenticity, hermeneutic analysis, and historical-geopolitical precedent). The paper concludes without breaking the tie among the ten alternatives, arguing that genuine uncertainty is intellectually more honest than a premature conclusion, and proposes, as a deliberately declared speculation, that ETIs themselves — if technologically advanced but not omnipotent — may share with humanity the same fundamental uncertainty about the future.

items.title: Occupational fatigue in bakery workers: A retrospective analysis of physical workplace factors in 2019
items.abstract: Occupational fatigue is an important occupational health concern that may reduce workers’ performance and increase the risk of workplace accidents. This study aimed to analyze the associations between physical workplace factors and occupational fatigue among bakery workers in Indonesia. This quantitative analytical observational study used a cross-sectional design and was conducted at a bakery factory CV “X” in Kampar Regency, Riau Province, Indonesia, in 2019. A total of 55 workers were recruited using total sampling. Workplace illumination, noise, temperature, and vibration were measured using environmental monitoring instruments, whereas occupational fatigue was assessed using the Work Fatigue Feeling Measurement Questionnaire (KAUPK2). Data were analyzed using chi-square tests and multiple logistic regression. Of the 55 workers, 38 (69.09%) experienced occupational fatigue. Bivariate analysis showed significant associations between fatigue and illumination (p = 0.004), noise (p = 0.001), and vibration (p = 0.006), whereas temperature was not significantly associated with fatigue (p = 0.170). In the multivariable analysis, illumination (POR = 0.124, 95% CI: 0.021–0.726; p = 0.021) and noise (POR = 8.381, 95% CI: 1.093–64.256; p = 0.041) remained significantly associated with occupational fatigue. Occupational fatigue was prevalent among bakery workers and was associated with workplace illumination and noise. Improving workplace lighting and controlling noise exposure should be considered in occupational health and safety programs.

items.title: OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH HAZARDS ASSOCIATED WITH TEACHING PROFESSION AS PERCEIVED BY SECONDARY SCHOOL TEACHERS IN AWKA EDUCATION ZONE
items.abstract: The study investigated occupational hazards associated with the teaching profession as perceived by secondary school teachers in Awka Education Zone of Anambra State. The study was guided by four research questions and four null hypotheses, which were tested at the 0.05 level of significance. A descriptive survey research design was adopted for the study. The study was conducted in Awka Education Zone. The zone has 65 public secondary schools with a total teacher population of 1,689. From this population, a sample of 304 teachers was selected using a simple random sampling technique. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire. Three education and measurement experts validated the instrument, and its reliability was established using Cronbach's alpha. The overall reliability index was 0.74. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, while independent-samples t-tests were applied to test the null hypotheses. The findings revealed that respondents perceived physical, biological, psychosocial, and ergonomic hazards as associated with the teaching profession. Additionally, male and female teachers showed no significant differences in mean ratings across all four hazard categories. Based on the findings, it was concluded that occupational hazards are prevalent in the teaching profession in Awka Education Zone and that both male and female teachers are equally affected. The study recommended that, among other things, secondary schools train and deploy health and safety officers to monitor and mitigate biological hazards. Schools should establish and maintain hygienic practices, provide clean water and sanitation facilities, and ensure that teachers are adequately protected from communicable diseases through timely health education and medical check-ups.

items.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
items.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce \textbf{Omni-InteractScope}, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) \textbf{Timely tool invocation remains unreliable}: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) \textbf{Query-free reminders remain poorly covered}: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) \textbf{End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited}: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.

items.title: Oncology networks and clinical care pathways in contemporary surgical oncology: between appropriateness, governance, and the sustainability of clinical practice
items.abstract: Background: Technological innovation is transforming endocrine surgery through new diagnostic and therapeutic tools that enhance precision, safety, and personalization of care. However, their clinical value depends on appropriate integration into evidence-based care pathways. This review summarizes the scientific discussions presented during the session “Innovations in Endocrine Surgery” at the 44th National Congress of the Italian Association of Hospital Surgeons, Palermo, Italy, 24–27 May 2026. Methods: A narrative review was conducted of presentations addressing ultrasound-guided thermal ablation, intraoperative neuromonitoring, lymphadenectomy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, intraoperative parathyroid identification, robotic and remote-access thyroid surgery, and laparoscopic versus robotic adrenalectomy. Session transcripts were analyzed according to the methodology described by Molteni et al. Findings were critically interpreted using current international guidelines and primary literature. Results: A consistent message emerged across all topics. Thermal ablation, near-infrared autofluorescence, neuromonitoring, and robotic platforms expand the technical possibilities of endocrine surgery by improving precision, safety, ergonomics, and, in selected patients, quality of life. However, their benefits consistently depended on three factors: appropriate patient selection, surgical expertise, and treatment within high-volume multidisciplinary centers. These principles were evident across thyroid, parathyroid, and adrenal surgery. Conclusions: Innovation in endocrine surgery derives its value not from technology itself, but from its appropriate application to individual patients. Although technological advances broaden surgical capabilities, clinical outcomes remain primarily determined by sound judgment, surgical expertise, and organization of care. Technology should therefore be regarded as an adjunct to, rather than a substitute for, high-quality clinical decision-making.

items.title: OpenEvidence versus Six Leading Large Language Models in Refractive Surgery: Does Curated Medical Evidence Confer an Advantage?
items.abstract: PURPOSE: To assess the accuracy of OpenEvidence relative to six leading large language models (LLMs) in answering refractive surgery multiple-choice questions, and to compare their performance with users of the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Basic and Clinical Science Course (BCSC) Self-Assessment Program. SETTING: Not applicable. DESIGN: Randomized questionnaire-based study using 225 questions from the refractive surgery section of the AAO BCSC Program. METHODS: OpenEvidence and 6 LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, and Grok) answered the same set of multiple-choice questions. Their accuracy was defined as the proportion of correct responses. Performance from 1,983 BCSC Self-Assessment Program users served as a benchmark. RESULTS: OpenEvidence achieved the lowest accuracy (76%) and performed significantly worse (P<0.05) than all six general-purpose LLMs. Claude achieved the highest accuracy (92%), followed by Grok (89.8%). ChatGPT-5, Copilot, and Gemini each scored an accuracy of 88%, and ChatGPT-4o achieved 86.2%. All models' lower 95% confidence interval bounds exceeded the 60% passing threshold. The average score of BCSC Self-Assessment Program users was 77%. All general-purpose LLMs scored significantly higher than BCSC Self-Assessment Program users (P<0.05), whereas OpenEvidence did not. CONCLUSIONS: OpenEvidence demonstrated significantly lower accuracy than the six evaluated general-purpose LLMs and did not exceed the BCSC Self-Assessment program user benchmark on this standardized refractive surgery multiple-choice assessment. This task-specific difference was not fully explained by response-format noncompliance and should not be interpreted as direct evidence of globally inferior medical knowledge or performance in open-ended clinical applications.

items.title: Operationalization and Use of PRISM Since 2020: An Updated Citation Analysis and Scoping Review
items.abstract: This project contains the protocol and supporting materials for an updated citation analysis and scoping review of the Practical, Robust Implementation and Sustainability Model (PRISM). The first scoping review of PRISM (Rabin et al., 2022) covered its use from 2008 through September 2020. This review extends that work by characterizing how PRISM has been used, operationalized, and applied since October 2020, including applications focused on health equity and expansion into new fields, settings, and methods. The review also has a methodological aim: to describe and evaluate the use of artificial intelligence to support the scoping review process, comparing AI-assisted, AI plus human, and human-only workflows on accuracy and time at the full text screening, use type classification, and data abstraction stages. Records were identified through six database searches, reverse citation analyses of five index PRISM publications, and colleague recommendation, and are managed in Covidence. Reporting will follow the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR).

items.title: Opportunity in the Age of Agents: How Generative AI Changes Opportunity Recognition, Evaluation and Creation
items.abstract: Entrepreneurship theory explains how opportunities are recognised, evaluated and created, but it models every stage of that process as exclusively human. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now participates in all three stages: founders use large language models as co-ideators that generate opportunity candidates and as drafting partners that develop them, while investors use the same class of models to screen founders' submissions. This conceptual paper integrates opportunity theory (discovery, creation and effectuation) with the emerging empirical evidence on generative AI and ideation, creativity, evaluation and entrepreneurial performance. It argues that the co-ideator changes the opportunity process in four ways: it expands each founder's supply of candidates while compressing ideation skill gaps; it correlates opportunity pools across founders who draw on shared models, creating a homogenisation risk at market level; it raises the returns to prior knowledge, which governs selection among abundant machine-generated candidates; and it migrates durable advantage from generating opportunities to selecting, combining and enacting them. These claims are stated as seven formal propositions with boundary conditions, including the "jagged opportunity frontier" and the evaluation asymmetries produced by narrative AI explanations, with implications for founders, investors and educators, and a research agenda.

items.title: Optical Speckle Patterns as Nonlinear Feature Maps for Photonic Machine Learning
items.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for energy-efficient hardware, and optical computing has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional electronic processors owing to its high parallelism and potentially lower power consumption. In this work, we investigate an optical computing architecture based on an integrated photonic circular multipass cell, focusing on its suitability for machine learning and pattern recognition tasks. The properties of the system are evaluated through measures of nonlinearity and cosine similarity, which characterize the system's information-processing capacity and the dimensionality of the generated feature representations. Numerical results demonstrate that the reservoir mirror reflectance, the size of the encoded figure, and the refractive-index contrast between the reservoir and the encoded figure modify the nonlinearity of the system, as verified via pairwise similarity estimates. These results indicate that the features generated by the circular multipass cell can be tailored by adjusting the system parameters, providing a means to control the reservoir transformation of the input data. The resulting representations were applied to classification tasks involving texture images and thyroid collagen images, achieving classification accuracies ranging from 69% to 93%. These findings suggest that photonic computing systems could provide a basis for more energy-efficient machine-learning hardware.

items.abstract: This community service program concerned the preparation of AI-assisted teaching modules for teachers at SDN 07 Srengseng Sawah, South Jakarta. The partner assessment described constraints related to teachers’ time, understanding of teaching-module components, access to contextual examples, and limited experience in using AI for instructional planning. The main workshop took place on 3 October 2025. The activity report described preparation and coordination, delivery of materials, practical sessions using generative AI tools, direct assistance, and documentation. The reported outputs comprised teaching modules developed by teachers or teacher groups, a collection of prompts and templates, and guidance on reviewing AI-generated materials responsibly. Photographs in the report document the presentation session and direct assistance to teachers. Although the final report states that teachers’ digital literacy and AI-use skills increased, it does not present individual test scores, participant totals, or numerical pre- and post-test summaries. Accordingly, this article reports the implementation and outputs descriptively, without quantifying a learning gain. The experience illustrates the use of practical training and guidance to support teaching-module preparation while maintaining teachers’ role in validating instructional materials.

items.title: Optimización de la cosecha en palma de aceite: productividad laboral, factores determinantes y alternativas tecnológicas
items.abstract: Harvesting is the most labor-intensive task in oil palm cultivation, accounting for 14–17% of production costs. The growing shortage of workers has driven the search for technological alternatives and process optimization; therefore, this study conducted a systematic review to identify factors influencing labor productivity and assess available technologies. Scientific databases were consulted, and 75 relevant publications were selected. Results indicate that harvesting involves three stages (cutting, collection, and lifting), with technological configurations achieving labor productivity between 0.97 and 3.5 t FFB/man-day depending on the level of harvests system mechanization. However, labor productivity is not determined solely by technology but by the interaction of three factors: labor (skills and ergonomic conditions), crop (yield, palm height, accessibility, and climate), and technology (mechanization level and support infrastructure). Emerging trends include mature solutions for in-field transport, intermediate developments in ergonomics and logistics optimization, early-stage research and innovation on full automation.

items.title: Optimization of Advertising Bidding Model With Generative AI and Deep Reinforcement Learning Collaboration: Design and Validation of Closed‐Loop Simulation Framework
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Real‐time bidding (RTB) requires decisions in milliseconds under nonstationary market dynamics; traditional optimization and online RL suffer from sample efficiency, stability and generalization limitations. This study proposes a closed‐loop simulation framework coupling generative AI with deep reinforcement learning. A cascaded encoder combining a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) with a denoising diffusion probability model (DDPM) synthesizes high‐fidelity market states. A proximal policy optimization (PPO) agent trains in this environment via a three‐stage ‘generate, evaluate, optimize’ mechanism, with a dynamic feedback regulator forming a co‐evolutionary loop. Experiments on 47.82 million anonymized bidding records improve CTR by 23.7%, CVR by 31.2%, ROI by 23.5% over DQN and increase ROI by 6.1% over GAVE and 8.6% over DiffBid. A 2 × 2 factorial ablation confirms significant generator‐agent interaction ( = 0.37 ROI units, 95% CI [0.24, 0.51], = 0.008, = 0.024). Cross‐dataset transfer on iPinYou preserves rankings with 7.0% ROI advantage over GAVE; counterfactual OPE on real logs (SNIPS, doubly robust, auction replay) agrees with simulator ranking. The system achieves 87.4% sample utilization (distinct from GPU utilization 92.30%) and 14.8 ms mean inference latency (p50/p95/p99 = 12.4/18.7/23.1 ms; 100% SLA at 100,000 req/s). A live A/B test on a production platform is planned as future work.

items.title: Organisational Conditions for Healthcare Workers' Wellbeing: The Roles of Leadership, Social Climate and Psychosocial Safety Climate
items.abstract: AIM: To assess a comprehensive model linking servant leadership, health-promoting leadership, workplace social climate, psychosocial safety climate, work conditions and healthcare workers' wellbeing. DESIGN: A cross-sectional survey design. METHODS: A total of 1563 healthcare workers completed a survey between 2024 and 2025. Structural equation modelling was employed to test the hypothesised relationships. RESULTS: Servant leadership, health-promoting leadership and workplace social climate were positively associated with healthcare workers' perceptions of psychosocial safety climate. Higher levels of psychosocial safety climate were linked to lower cognitive job demands and greater job resources, including job control, supervisor support and colleague support. These work conditions were associated with lower psychological strain and turnover intention, as well as higher job satisfaction and work engagement. Unexpectedly, cognitive job demands were positively related to work engagement, suggesting that cognitively challenging work may be perceived as meaningful and motivating in healthcare settings. CONCLUSIONS: Supportive leadership and a positive workplace social climate are important correlates of psychosocial safety climate, which was associated with healthier work conditions and better wellbeing among healthcare workers. In addition, the findings suggest that certain job demands may play a motivational as well as a straining role in healthcare contexts. IMPLICATIONS: Strengthening leadership practices and cultivating a supportive workplace social climate help healthcare organisations foster psychosocial safety climate and improve work conditions for healthcare workers. Enhancing these conditions supports healthcare workers' wellbeing and is associated with more sustainable healthcare workplaces. REPORTING METHOD: The STROBE checklist. items.title: Parental perceptions and the development of the AI-integrated digital home literacy environment among English as a foreign language learners
items.abstract: With the widespread use of technology in children's home learning, the home literacy environment (HLE) has been gradually digitalized, and the digital home literacy environment (DHLE) is put forward based on the HLE framework. However, the components and developmental dynamics of DHLE remain underexplored. Guided by the theory of planned behavior, this qualitative study investigated the components of the DHLE for English as a foreign language learners and how it is informed by parents’ perceptions. Data were collected from eight families through semi-structured interviews with both fathers and mothers of children aged 5–6 years, and hybrid thematic analysis was employed. Findings showed that the DHLE comprised digital and artificial intelligence (AI) devices and related resources, digital and AI-assisted language learning activities, and parental mediation strategies. Parents’ attitudes toward digital and AI-assisted learning, subjective norms including cultural values and societal influence, and perceived behavioral control, including parents’ time and resource constraints, digital and AI literacy, and English proficiency, jointly informed their intentions to support children's digital English learning, thereby influencing DHLE. The study extends the theoretical understanding of HLE by introducing a digital facet. It highlights the importance of parental mediation in children's language learning with digital technologies and contributes to the research on AI-supported education by exploring its application in home language learning environments, an area that has received limited attention. The study has implications for practice and policy in digital early childhood education.

items.title: Patient preferences for portable versus table-mounted visual field devices in rural Alabama: A mixed methods study within a telemedicine setting
items.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate patient satisfaction and preferences for portable versus table-mounted visual field (VF) devices in a rural telemedicine setting and identify influencing factors. METHODS: We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed methods study at three Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) within the Alabama Screening and Intervention for Glaucoma and eye Health through Telemedicine (AL-SIGHT) study. Participants completed VF testing with table-mounted Humphrey Field Analyzer (HFA), tablet-based Melbourne Rapid Fields (MRF), and virtual reality (VR)-based VisuALL perimeters. Participants rated satisfaction, comfort, ease of use, and future testing preference. Chi-square tests assessed differences in device preferences. Twelve participants completed semi-structured interviews to explore reasons underlying preferences. Qualitative data were analyzed in NVivo 14 using reflexive thematic analysis. RESULTS: Among 271 respondents (mean age 60.4 years; 62.4% women), 50.6% preferred VR-based, 35.1% tablet-based, and 14.4% table-mounted for future testing (χ2 (2) = 53.52, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.31). Satisfaction was highest for VR-based (56.9% very satisfied), followed by tablet-based (49.4%), and HFA (38.0%). VR-based perimeter was most frequently selected as the most comfortable (55.7%; χ2 (2) = 63.33, p < 0.001, V = 0.34) and easiest to use (54.6%; χ2 (2) = 71.96, p < 0.001, V = 0.36). Preferences did not vary significantly across demographic variables (all p > 0.05). Qualitative themes identified four key drivers: comfort and physical experience, visual experience, ease of use and interaction, and psychological and motivational factors. Portability and community suitability were valued. CONCLUSION: Rural underserved patients strongly preferred portable visual field devices, particularly VR-based, over table-mounted HFA. Comfort, ergonomic flexibility, immersive visual experience, and simplicity of interaction were central determinants of preference. Portable perimetry may enhance patient-centered glaucoma monitoring within telemedicine programs and access in resource-limited settings.

items.title: Patient-initiated conversational AI between appointments in breast cancer care: a multidisciplinary clinical and policy perspective
items.abstract: General-purpose conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for health-related questions, including questions relevant to cancer care, although breast-cancer-specific prevalence and behavioural effects remain poorly characterised. Most evaluations ask whether an AI answer is accurate. That is necessary but incomplete. Clinically consequential effects may arise when a fluent, apparently personalised exchange changes a treatment preference, delays contact with the clinical team, reinforces reassurance-seeking, validates non-adherence, or converts population guidance into an individual-sounding instruction. We conceptualise this as a parallel pathway: an AI-mediated sequence of questions, answers and actions that is usually invisible to the treating team, absent from the medical record and unattached to professional responsibility, yet capable of re-entering formal care through its downstream consequences. We distinguish model error from pathway error and propose traceability, reversibility, and returnability to accountable care as safety properties beyond answer accuracy. Across four clinical domains, we propose distinct pathway failure modes: premature preference closure in surgical decision-making; escalation closure during treatment toxicity; repetitive reassurance-seeking and over-reliance in psycho-oncology; and loss of conditionality in perioperative recovery and lifestyle advice. These are hypothesis-generating mechanisms rather than empirically established dominant patterns. We propose a five-step clinical response - ASK, RECONSTRUCT, CLASSIFY, CHECK and RETURN - based on non-judgemental inquiry, proportionate documentation and explicit return-to-care boundaries. Regulation can govern products and deployed systems, but it cannot by itself reveal patient-initiated consumer AI use. Clinical services therefore need governance for the pathway as well as for the technology.

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than tracking how clinical responsibilities evolve across a longitudinal care pathway. Here we introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from longitudinal records of 405 patients across two cancer centers, the benchmark comprises 941 patient-phase units across six sequential care phases and 17,688 patient-specific atomic criteria spanning five evaluation dimensions, with each assessment strictly restricted to decision-time clinical evidence. Evaluating 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs revealed that strong diagnostic performance does not carry over to downstream care. We evaluated 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, showing that high diagnostic performance did not translate into improved downstream care. Instead, the dominant failure modes reversed across phases. Explicit decision errors dominated anatomical staging at 48.2%, whereas decision omissions dominated initial work-up and post-treatment follow-up at 33.4% and 30.4%, respectively. In the evaluated model set, medically adapted models showed higher omission rates than general-purpose models. Moreover, varying query granularity exposes a critical specification trade-off: broad open-ended requests degrade Decision Quality across all 30 models, while more detailed, checklist-like prompts raise Decision Quality but reduce Evidence Faithfulness and Safety Adherence. Furthermore, NPC-RubricBench demonstrates that static diagnostic benchmarks are insufficient to ensure consistent clinical reliability over time, highlighting the importance of phase-adaptive safeguards in multistage medical AI.

items.title: Pedagogical resilience reconstruction in the AI era: a longitudinal reflexive thematic analysis of teacher reflective journals
items.abstract: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) lowers the threshold for producing work, not necessarily for learning. This study examines how an instructor kept an interdisciplinary AI course teachable for first-year art students, where that effort reached its limits, and how the instructor interpreted students' engagement with AI tools. Methods The study is a longitudinal practitioner self-study of a 12-week course taught in autumn 2025 at a higher vocational college in northwestern China. The data are the instructor's own reflective journals: structured entries written during the semester for Weeks 1–7 and retrospective accounts of Weeks 8–12 written after the semester ended. The two strata are reported separately. Reflexive thematic analysis produced 40 evidence anchors, five themes, one cross-cutting thread, and one central organizing theme, with a full audit trail. Results The instructor's repairs (translating content into everyday and discipline-specific tasks, working around broken or restricted lab equipment, and demonstrating on the teacher's computer) kept the course running. However, as content moved toward frontier tools that required paid accounts, computing resources, and prior AI experience, teaching drifted toward demonstration (“the more cutting-edge something is, the more it can only be demonstrated”). Across the semester the instructor recorded a recurring pattern, here termed a teacher-perceived low-threshold illusion , in which students appeared, in the instructor's account, to treat seeing, bookmarking, or one-click generation as equivalent to being able to do. The instructor associated this pattern with three co-occurring conditions: natural-language prompting and one-click generation, demonstration-only teaching, and a final assessment that students could complete without having attended. Participation could be high while, in the instructor's judgement, students gained little. Conclusion Pedagogical resilience reconstruction in AI teaching is bounded. Keeping an AI course running did not by itself make learning visible: the journals record a tension between engagement, product completion, and evidence of learning, not an established failure of learning. In-course repair reached limits shaped by access conditions and an inherited assessment format, and reconstruction of the course took place at the scale of the semester. We present pedagogical resilience reconstruction as an emerging construct for multi-case testing.

items.title: Penerapan Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Analisis Pengaduan Berbasis LLM, dan Peramalan Indikator Sosial Ekonomi pada Portal BAPPEDA Kota Pariaman
items.abstract: The BAPPEDA portal of Pariaman City previously served planning documents only as downloadable files, stored public complaints without processing, and offered no socioeconomic indicator data. During an internship at the Communication and Informatics Office of Pariaman City (1–31 July 2026), three artificial intelligence models were integrated into the portal through incremental development. First, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) question-answering model combines gemini-embedding-001 vectors, cosine similarity, a similarity threshold, and Gemini 2.5 Flash with schema-constrained JSON output. Second, a zero-shot Large Language Model (LLM) analyses each complaint in the background and recommends category fit, sentiment, and urgency without sending the complainant’s identity. Third, linear regression, ARIMA, and Prophet forecast the Human Development Index (HDI), poverty rate, open unemployment rate, and Gini ratio of Pariaman City; the best method per indicator is selected by backtesting, with linear regression as a fallback. An evaluation with 40 test questions moved the threshold from 0.65 to 0.74, which gave the highest balanced accuracy (62.9%) and raised out-of-scope rejection from 14.3% to 64.3%, while recall@5 fell from 92.3% to 61.5%. Backtesting showed that linear regression was most accurate for HDI (MAPE 0.44%), whereas ARIMA was best for the other three indicators (MAPE 3.80–8.19%). All 18 automated feature tests passed. The models turn the portal into an interactive service that supports information retrieval, complaint prioritisation, and development planning.

items.title: Pengaruh Video Pembelajaran Kreatif terhadap Motivasi Belajar Generasi Z dalam Pendidikan Sejarah Islam
items.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between creative learning videos and learning motivation among Generation Z students in the context of Islamic history education. Using a quantitative approach with correlational design, this research involved 30 students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using two main instruments: the Creative Learning Video Usage Questionnaire (CLVUQ) and Learning Motivation Scale (LMS), both demonstrating high reliability with Cronbach's alpha values of 0.906 and 0.942, respectively. The findings reveal a weak positive correlation (R = 0.340) between creative learning video usage and learning motivation, with an explanatory power of 11.6% (R Square = 0.116). A notably high acceptance rate of creative learning videos was reflected by 93.33% of respondents providing positive responses, with an average satisfaction score of 4.37 (SD = 0.62). Further analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation emerged as the most responsive dimension, with an average score of 4.12, compared to extrinsic motivation (3.89) and self-efficacy (4.01). These findings underscore the importance of integrating traditional and modern learning approaches in Islamic history education while emphasizing the need to consider contextual factors such as social, cultural, and institutional aspects in developing technology-based learning strategies. Despite certain methodological limitations, this research provides meaningful empirical foundations for developing more effective learning strategies in the digital era, particularly in the context of Islamic history education for Generation Z.

items.title: PERCEIVED INFLUENCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON COMPUTATIONAL SKILLS AND MATHEMATICAL REASONING AMONG PRE-SERVICE TEACHERS IN NASARAWA STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study examined perceived influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on computational skills and independent reasoning among pre-service teachers in College of Education, Akwanga, Nasarawa State. Five research questions and three hypotheses guided the study. Descriptive survey design was adopted. Population was 125 NCE mathematics pre-service teachers, sample was 100 (62 males, 38 females) selected by simple random sampling. Instrument was Artificial Intelligence on Computational Skills and Mathematical Reasoning among Pre-Service Teachers (AI-CSMRPT) with reliability of 0.82 Cronbach Alpha. Mean and SD answered research questions, one-way ANOVA and one-sample t-test tested hypotheses at 0.05. Findings revealed AI significantly influences computational skills (Grand M=3.09) by improving speed (M=3.24) and accuracy (M=3.18). Both male (M=3.18) and female (M=2.95) agreed, but significant gender difference existed (F=4.67 > 3.94). AI also influences independent reasoning (Grand M=2.90), with reliance on AI before attempting problems (M=3.16) highest. Both genders agreed (M=2.98 male, M=2.77 female) with significant difference (F=4.12 > 3.94). No significant difference between influence on computational skills (M=3.09) and independent reasoning (M=2.90), p=0.47. Study concluded AI enhances computation but creates alternative cognition that reduces independent effort if unguided. Responsible and ethical use of AI as supplement, gender-sensitive training, and institutional guidelines were recommended.

items.title: Personal data anonymization in the context of artificial intelligence: from de-Identification to anonymization
items.abstract: Background . The processing of medical data by artificial intelligence (AI) systems requires mandatory de-identification, yet simple removal of direct identifiers does not ensure anonymity. Modern AI models can re-identify individuals from indirect attributes, leaving a measurable residual risk. Objective . The aim of this study was to define the boundaries of de-identification in the AI era, systematize protection methods, and assess the actual attitudes of future physicians toward patient data handling. Methods . We conducted an anonymous cross-sectional survey of 1,283 medical university students and residents (me dian age 21 years). A self-administered questionnaire was used. Data were analyzed in Python (pandas) using chi-squared tests and Cramér’s V to compare differences across training levels. Results . Entering de-identified clinical text into cloud-based AI services was considered acceptable by 61.5 % of respon dents; 12.4 % had already uploaded real patient data, with 1.2 % doing so in identifiable form. Awareness of risks did not deter risky behavior: those who uploaded data had higher self-assessed risk knowledge (3.53 vs. 3.36, p < 0.0001), and 22 % admitted their actions were unacceptable yet continued them. The proportion of uploaders increased from 7.5 % in junior years to 21.0 % in senior years (χ² = 43.3, Cramér’s V = 0.18, p < 0.0001), while willingness to inform patients about AI use declined from 43.4 % to 24.4 %. Conclusions . Anonymity is not a state to be achieved but a continuous process of managing residual re-identification risk. Effective protection requires institutional bans on sharing de-identified data with public cloud services, adoption of methods with quantifiable residual risk (differential privacy, federated learning, homomorphic encryption), and strengthening education al curricula on ethics and information security.

items.title: Perspective Chapter: Governing the Autonomous Fortress – Multi-Agent AI Systems for Secure and Resilient Cloud Cybersecurity
items.abstract: Cybersecurity is changing from reactive, human-centered systems to highly autonomous cyber-capable agents (HACCAs) that can operate at machine speed and scale. This chapter introduces the Autonomous Fortress, an architectural framework that changes artificial intelligence from a tool that only supports analysis into a system that can make decisions, plan multiple steps, use different tools, and improve its actions through continuous reasoning. The core of the Autonomous Fortress is a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). In this system, specialized agents for perception, correlation, analysis, and response work together as digital teammates to protect the environment. The framework combines different coordination methods, including a hierarchical supervisor model and swarm-based dynamic handoff, to support adaptive and context-aware decision-making. This approach goes beyond traditional machine learning systems that mainly depend on fixed rules and pattern matching. Although these secure-by-design mechanisms improve the defender’s ability to respond to cyber threats, high levels of autonomy also introduce new risks, such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascading system failures. Based on national cybersecurity strategies and enterprise deployments from 2025 to 2026, this chapter presents both a technical and governance roadmap for building secure and resilient autonomous cyber defense systems in modern digital and cloud-native environments.

items.title: PHARMACOGENOMICS AND PRECISION MEDICINE IN PHARMACY PRACTICE: CURRENT EVIDENCE, CLINICAL APPLICATIONS, IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGIES, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
items.abstract: Pharmacogenomics (PGx) is an important component of precision medicine that uses genetic information to explain interindividual variability in medication response. Its clinical value is greatest when a validated genetic result can be translated into a specific therapeutic action, such as selection of an alternative drug, dose adjustment, intensified monitoring, or avoidance of a medicine associated with severe toxicity. The role of pharmacy practice is expanding because pharmacists possess expertise in pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, medication safety, medication therapy management, patient counseling, and longitudinal follow-up. This review examines the current role of pharmacogenomics in pharmacy practice, including clinically actionable gene–drug relationships, pharmacist-led testing, community and hospital implementation, electronic health record (EHR) integration, clinical decision support, medication safety, health equity, ethics, pharmacoeconomics, and future research. Evidence from pharmacogenomic implementation literature, Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) guidance, and regulatory resources was considered. Important examples include CYP2C19–clopidogrel, CYP2D6–opioids and selected antidepressants, DPYD–fluoropyrimidines, TPMT/NUDT15–thiopurines, HLA-B–abacavir, HLA-B–carbamazepine and allopurinol, SLCO1B1–statins, CYP3A5–tacrolimus, and VKORC1/CYP2C9/CYP4F2–warfarin. Pharmacists can contribute across the complete PGx pathway: identifying candidates, arranging testing, interpreting results, documenting genotype/phenotype, recommending evidence-based medication changes, communicating with prescribers, counseling patients, monitoring outcomes, and evaluating service quality. Contemporary implementation studies indicate that community-pharmacy delivery is feasible and generally acceptable, but barriers include pharmacist knowledge and confidence, reimbursement, workflow integration, interoperability, standardized guidance, privacy, and equitable access. A successful precision-pharmacy model should therefore combine pharmacogenomic information with clinical phenotype, comorbidities, organ function, concomitant medicines, patient preferences, and therapeutic monitoring. Future pharmacy research should emphasize prospective clinical outcomes, cost-effectiveness, implementation science, Indian population data, diverse genomic representation, and responsible artificial-intelligence-supported clinical decision support.

items.abstract: Abstract In recent years, Western philosophical inquiry has expanded beyond its traditional focus on humans, exploring questions about other‐ and more‐than human beings. This movement addresses a diverse array of topics, considering animals and elements of the natural world as well as growing attention to artificial intelligence. The resulting special issue includes four articles that explore pedagogical relationships between humans and nonhuman or more‐than‐human entities (Hamilton, Krabbe, Lussier, and Pedersen), with two focused specifically on technology (Anderson and Khan). Together this set of articles offers insights into philosophy of education beyond the human that engage with a rich array of traditions of thought in philosophy and educational theory.

items.title: PhysAgent: A Multi-Agent Large Language Model Framework for Physics Data Analysis and Simulation
items.abstract: Abstract The inference of physical laws has traditionally relied on human intuition, analytical reasoning, and experimental observation. However, modern physics research is increasingly constrained by challenges such as high specialization, fragmented workflows, and limited computational resources, which impede scientific progress. To address these issues, we introduce PhysAgent , a novel multi-agent system powered by large language models (LLMs), designed to execute end-to-end scientific workflows—from hypothesis generation and computational modeling to data analysis and reporting. PhysAgent’s innovation lies in its specialized agent collaboration: a Mentor Agent guides scientific reasoning through Socratic questioning, a Student Agent handles technical execution (e.g., code implementation, DFT calculations), and a Leader Agent dynamically optimizes task scheduling and resource allocation. Integrating domain-specific tools like first-principles simulations (e.g., Quantum ESPRESSO, VASP), PhysAgent aims to improve reproducibility while maintaining human-in-the-loop refinement. We demonstrate PhysAgent as a proof-of-concept framework for recovering known physical relations from controlled data, including Kepler-law recovery from orbital trajectories and Newton-law recovery from force-motion data. Furthermore, it extends to ab initio materials modeling, automating electronic structure workflows (e.g., GaAs band-structure and density-of-states calculations). In addition, PhysAgent simulates complex real-world phenomena, such as raindrop flow on train windows. By harmonizing LLM-driven planning with domain-specific tools, PhysAgent provides a reproducible multi-agent workflow for physics data analysis and simulation. We provide a demonstration video of PhysAgent to illustrate its workflow and capabilities: https://b23.tv/emOilkC.

items.title: Phytonanoparticles for food safety and preservation: potential role, evidence and challenges in antimicrobial resistance mitigation
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global threat to humankind, affecting food safety, health, and the economy. Moreover, it is evolving rapidly, resulting from the misuse and overuse of antibiotics in healthcare and agriculture a result which has emerged as a One Health challenge. It alters food systems by creating threats to food safety, food security, and public health. Such resistant microorganisms have the ability to persist and spread in the food systems, animals, water, and the environment. Such microorganisms are further sustained by the production of biofilms. There is increased demand for safe and sustainable alternatives as a result of the limited applicability of conventional antibiotics and chemical preservatives. Plant-mediated phyto-nanoparticles (PNPs) are emerging antimicrobials. A PRISMA-compliant literature search and bibliometric analysis were used to identify leading research trends and gaps. This review evaluates their applicability in different aspects of food safety and preservation and in mitigating AMR. It includes major foodborne pathogens, resistance mechanisms, biofilm formation, and synthesis of bioactive nanoparticles using plants. The main antimicrobial mechanisms of these nanoparticles include the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), disruption of the cell membrane, release of metal ions, enzyme inhibition, DNA damage, and interference with quorum sensing. This review includes their applicability in active food packaging, edible coatings, food preservation, and food processing surfaces. This review expands existing research by including the results of real food matrices and storage studies. The review incorporates the emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in nanoparticles design, prediction of antimicrobial activities, and optimization of synthesis parameters, and trend identification. In general, PNPs have a lot of potential for sustainable approaches to food preservation. However, standardized methods, rigorous safety evaluation, AI/ML-assisted optimization, and real-food, in vivo , and industrial studies are needed for successful translation.

items.title: PolicyMediator: Multi-Regional Policy Learning through Mediation Agents with Evolving Skills in OPC Ecosystems
items.abstract: One-person companies (OPCs) are emerging enterprises operated by individual entrepreneurs through digital platforms and LLM-based AI agents. These highly skilled entrepreneurs are characterized by being digital nomads, with limited reliance on local ecosystems. Governments in China use distinct regional support policies to attract mobile OPCs, turning local support into a cross-regional coordination problem. OPCs compare regions to maximize their own utility, but imperfect policy perceptions may cause them to reject otherwise suitable locations. Existing policy-learning methods optimize resources under fixed perceptions, while consensus-formation methods aggregate views without feeding cognitive changes back into policy learning. This disconnect produces mismatched location choices and inefficient regional policy adjustment. We introduce PolicyMediator, a cognition-constrained leader-multi-follower Stackelberg framework with bilateral mediation. The mediator explains verified policies to OPCs to build awareness and trust, and reports their needs and unresolved concerns to governments for policy learning. Its self-evolving skills retain, revise, or prune strategies using verification, allocation, capacity, and objective trajectories rather than mediation success alone. Across six-region simulations in China with five OPC types, five scenarios, and three OPC-simulator backbones, PolicyMediator ranks first in all 15 OPC-backbone--scenario combinations. Over the eight-baseline mean, it improves the aggregate government objective, combining economic performance, employment benefit, and policy-access equality, by 42.4% and average OPC utility by 40.9%.

items.title: POOJA RAMESH SINGH V. JAMMU & KASHMIR BANK LTD.: JUDICIAL INTEGRITY, AI-GENERATED AUTHORITIES AND THE LIMITS OF TECHNOLOGY IN ADJUDICATION
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence in research is growing. Artificial intelligence brings chances to work faster but it also brings worries about whether legal sources are correct and trustworthy. These worries were highlighted in the case Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. In that case the Supreme Court of India looked at how the National Company Law Tribunal trusted artificial intelligence–generated legal material. The main dispute was about enforcing a guarantee but the Supreme Court's decision asked a bigger question: can a judge rely on legal references that do not exist? This paper looks at the facts of the case the Supreme Court's reasoning and what it means for lawyers, judges and the entire legal field. It shows the difference between using intelligence as a helper for research and treating artificial intelligence's unverified output as an official law source. The paper also talks about lawyers' duty to check citations and the need for courts and tribunals to check whether the authorities they see are real. Even though artificial intelligence helps with research the paper says that technology cannot replace careful work or judicial responsibility. The Supreme Court decision reminds us that every legal decision must depend on proven legal sources. The decision also raises questions about punishments and the safety measures needed as artificial intelligence becomes more common in law practice. In the end the paper says that technology can help with thinking but human professionals must keep the responsibility, for accuracy and integrity of legal work.
